metric_rationale: The design was built so that on 12 of the 16 unique pairs (72 of 96 trials per subject) the tallies for A and B differ while the top-validity discriminating cue favors the option with FEWER feature wins — i.e., TTB and Tallying make strictly opposite predictions on every one of these trials (e.g., trial 2: A=[1,0,0,0,0] vs B=[0,1,1,0,0]; TTB picks A via cue 1, Tallying picks B via a 2-vs-1 tally; trial 15: cue 3 favors A but the tally is 1-vs-2 for B). The metric computes, purely from the observed choices, the proportion of these conflict trials on which the subject picked the TTB-favored option. Under TTB-simulated data this equals (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2 on every such trial — well above 0.5 for any non-trivial beta, and approaching ~1 for moderate/large beta. Under Tallying-simulated data it equals (1-eps)*(1 - sigmoid(margin*beta)) + eps/2 with margin >= 1 — well below 0.5, approaching ~eps/2 for moderate/large beta. So the two theories produce a large mean gap (typically 0.5-0.9 apart) in opposite directions. Crucially, the metric is a bounded proportion estimated from ~72 Bernoulli trials per subject, so per-subject sampling variance is tiny (<= p(1-p)/72 ~ 0.0035), making the between-subject variance small for both theories; with N=25 human subjects Welch's t-test on the (mean, variance) pairs will separate the theories decisively. The metric is computed generically from the ratings columns (cue cascade + tally counts recomputed row-wise), so it also runs unchanged on a single subject's slice, satisfying the per-subject variance requirement. Unlike a raw 'fit to TTB' measure, it is restricted to the double-dissociation trials where the two theories make opposite deterministic predictions, which is exactly where the design has maximal diagnostic leverage and where noise from the tie-trials (where Tallying guesses) cannot dilute the contrast.

The design's core dissociation is the CONFLICT cell: trials where the tally majority (the designated winner W) is opposed by the highest-validity discriminating cue. On those trials the two theories make opposite-signed predictions about P(choose W) for ANY noise parameters: Tallying gives P(W) = sigmoid(m*beta) with m >= 1, hence strictly > 0.5 (it obeys the cue majority even against the best cue); TTB gives P(W) = 1 - sigmoid(beta), hence strictly < 0.5 (it obeys the single top cue against the majority). So the metric P(W | conflict) - 0.5 is positive under Tallying and negative under TTB regardless of beta, epsilon, or which cue position d decides — the sign itself is diagnostic, and the magnitude grows with beta on both sides (the gap is (1-epsilon)*[weighted sigma(m*beta) + sigma(beta) - 1] over the 64 conflict trials per subject). This uses 64 of 96 trials per subject (conflict base trials 1,2,3,4,7,8,9,11,13,14,15,16,19,20,21,23 x 4 reps), giving tight per-subject estimates: e.g., at beta=1 the Tallying value is ~ +0.31 and the TTB value ~ -0.23 (gap ~0.55) with per-subject SD ~0.05-0.06, which at N=25 yields a Welch t in the dozens; even at the minimum beta=0.1 the gap (~0.07) still exceeds the per-subject noise (~0.018 SE). Congruent trials are deliberately excluded: at m=1 congruent both theories predict exactly sigmoid(beta), so they add variance without adding mean separation. The metric is computed identically on the pooled DataFrame and on single-subject slices (each subject has all 24 unique pairs), so between-subject variance is well defined. The classification (tally winner, top discriminating cue via the fixed descending-validity order) is recomputed from the raw ratings on every row, so no list-column hashing is needed.
